sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Hòuyì** (*houyi*) ​— Archery, Suns, ‌Heroism · The ‌divine archer who ​shot down nine ​suns — belongs ​to the Chinese tradition, ​where it is ​catalogued under the ‌domain "Archery, Suns, ​Heroism". The name ​means "The divine ‌archer who shot ​down nine suns"[^1].

‌**Hòuyì** is the ​divine archer of ‌Chinese myth, the ​hero who stood ​between heaven's excess ​and the earth's survival. ​In the age ​of the sage-emperor ‌Yáo, the ten ​suns — three-legged ‌crows, sons of ​Dìjùn and the ‌sun-mother Xīhé — ​rose all at ‌once instead of ​taking their appointed ‌turns. Rivers dried, ​crops failed, and monsters ​crawled out of ‌the scorched wilderness. ‌Hòuyì drew his ‌great bow and ​shot nine suns ​from the sky, ‌sparing one so ​that day and ​night, sowing and ‌harvest, could keep ​their order.

His ​story is a ‌hinge between worlds: the ​same bow that ‌cleared the earth ​of monsters also ​won him the ​elixir of immortality ​from Xīwángmǔ, the ‌Queen Mother of ‌the West — ​the elixir his ‌wife Cháng'é would ​ultimately take, fleeing ​to the moon. ‌The archer who saved ‌the earth lost ‌heaven, and Chinese ‌myth has never ​stopped telling both ‌halves of that ​story.[^2]

PuniCodex restores ​the name as ​**Hòuyì** and serves ‌its temple at ​[hòuyì.com](https://xn--huy-pma1a.com). The restoration ​preserves at least ​one distinctive feature — ‌a diacritic or ​a distinctive letter ​— that the ​ASCII form loses, ‌and exactly one ​historically valid Unicode ‌restoration exists, which ​places the name ‌in Tier 1. ​The plain ASCII ‌form *houyi* survives ‌as a modern ​convenience imposed by the ​early domain-name system; ​the restoration, not ​the fallback, is ‌the form the ‌project defends as ​philologically complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌Chinese ​characters as ​**后羿**. Etymologically ​it ​means "The ​divine archer ‌who ​shot down ​nine suns"[^1].

‌The ASCII ​form ‌*houyi* survives ​only because ‌the ​early domain-name ​system could ​not ​carry diacritics; ​it is ‌a ​technological compromise, ‌not an ​ancient ‌spelling. The ​Unicode restoration ‌**Hòuyì** ​recovers the ‌stress accent ​of ​the original ‌directly in ‌the address ‌bar. ​The restoration ​preserves at ‌least ​one distinctive ​feature — ‌a ​diacritic or ​a distinctive ‌letter ​— that ‌the ASCII ​form ​loses, and ​exactly one ​historically ‌valid Unicode ‌restoration exists, ​which ‌places the ​name in ​Tier 1.

‌The ‌letter-by-letter transformation ‌runs:

- ‌**h** ​→ **H** ‌— Same, ​capitalized
​- **o** ​→ **ò** ‌— ​Stress on ​o
- ​**u** ‌→ **u** ​— Same
​- ​**y** → ‌**y** — ​Same
‌- **i** ​→ **ì** ‌— Stress ​on ‌i

The ‌project holds ​the ​domain **hòuyì.com** ​(xn--huy-pma1a.com) as ​the ‌canonical home ‌of this ​name[^2].

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of ‌the name is ‌**/xoʊ̯˥˩.i˥˩/** — Modern ​Standard Mandarin ​(Pinyin).[^1]

Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- **hòu** ​— Syllable ​with voiceless velar ‌fricative [x] (Pinyin ​'h'), diphthongal ​final [oʊ̯] (Pinyin ‌'ou'), and ​Tone 4 (falling, ‌˥˩).
- **yì** ​— Syllable ‌with high front ​unrounded vowel [i] ​(Pinyin 'yi' ​writes a bare ​[i] with a ​glide onset), ‌and Tone 4 ​(falling, ˥˩).

‌For the modern ​speaker, the closest ‌approximation is: ​HOH-yee — two ‌crisp syllables, each ​spoken with ‌a sharp falling ​tone, like a ​decisive command: ‌'HOE! YEE!'

Kindred ‌and historical ‌forms of the ​name:

- **Traditional** ​— 后羿
‌- **Simplified** — ​后羿
- **Wade-Giles** ​— Hou⁴-i⁴
‌- **Cantonese (Jyutping)** ​— hau⁶ ji⁶
​- **Related ‌terms** — 十日 ​shí rì ‌(the ten suns); ​后羿射日 Hòuyì shè ​rì (Yi ​shoots the suns); ​嫦娥 Cháng'é (his ‌wife, the ‌moon goddess)

后羿 ​names the divine ‌archer: 后 ​is an archaic ​title meaning ‌'lord, sovereign' (not ‌the later sense ‌'empress', for ‌which 皇后 is ​used), and 羿 ‌is the ​archer's given name. ​The Modern Standard ​Mandarin reading ‌is Hòuyì (both ​syllables Tone ​4), as recorded ​in the Unihan ‌Database (Unicode ​Consortium, kMandarin) and ​standard Mandarin dictionaries. ​Baxter & ‌Sagart (2014) reconstruct ​the Old Chinese ‌reading of ​羿 as *N-ŋ(r)ik-s. ‌The tone-marked ​Pinyin restoration Hòuyì ‌preserves the citation ‌falling tone ​of both syllables; ​in connected speech ​the contour ​may be compressed, ‌but the lexical ‌tones remain ​Tone 4.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌written in ‌Chinese characters ​as **后羿**. ​This original ​script is ​the form ​against which ‌the ASCII ​fallback *houyi* ​and the ‌PuniCodex restoration ​**Hòuyì** are ‌measured: the ​restoration preserves ‌its pitch ​accent of ​the written ​form, so ​that a ​reader typing ‌the modern ​address still ‌speaks the ​ancient name.[^1]

‌The original ​script is ‌后羿, identical ​in ‌traditional and ​simplified Chinese ​(the character ‌后 'sovereign' ‌must not ‌be confused ​with 後 ​'after', which ‌simplifies to ​后 — ​in the ‌archer's name ​it is ​the archaic ‌title, 'lord'). ​Pinyin *Hòuyì* ‌(both syllables ​Tone 4) ​is the ​Modern Standard ​Mandarin reading, ‌recorded in ‌the Unihan ​Database and ‌standard dictionaries. ​The registrable ​Unicode restoration ‌uses the ‌tone-marked Pinyin ‌*Hòuyì* ‌rather than ​the hanzi ‌because PUNICODEX ​renders the ​original characters ​in the ‌temple's 'Original ​Script' card ​while keeping ​the domain ‌label pronounceable ​and internationally ​registrable; the ​name carries ‌no apostrophe, ​so the ‌display form ​and the ‌domain form ​differ only ‌in the ‌tone marks. ​Baxter & ​Sagart (2014) ​reconstruct the ​Old Chinese ‌reading of ‌羿 as ​*N-ŋ(r)ik-s.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Hòuyì** is ​the divine archer ‌of Chinese myth, ‌the hero who ​stood between heaven's ​excess and the ​earth's survival. In ​the age of ​the sage-emperor Yáo, ‌the ten suns ​— three-legged crows, ​sons of Dìjùn ‌and the sun-mother ​Xīhé — rose ‌all at once ​instead of ‌taking their appointed ​turns. Rivers dried, ​crops failed, and ​monsters crawled out ​of the scorched ​wilderness. Hòuyì drew ‌his great bow ​and shot nine ‌suns from the ​sky, sparing one ‌so that day ​and night, sowing ‌and harvest, could ​keep their order.

‌His story is ​a hinge between ​worlds: the same ‌bow that cleared ‌the earth of ‌monsters also won ​him the elixir ​of immortality from ‌Xīwángmǔ, the Queen ​Mother of the ​West — the ‌elixir his wife ​Cháng'é would ultimately ​take, fleeing to ‌the moon. ​The archer who ‌saved the earth ​lost heaven, and ​Chinese myth has ​never stopped telling ​both halves of ‌that story.[^1]

### ‌The Divine Bow

​The great bow ‌and its arrows ​are heaven's instruments ​of correction — ‌not conquest, but ‌the precise removal ‌of what has ‌grown excessive.

### ​The Ten Suns

‌Ten three-legged crow-suns, ​sons of Dìjùn ​and Xīhé, once ​took turns crossing ‌the sky; their ​simultaneous rising nearly ​ended the world.

​### Slayer of ‌Monsters

With the ​suns subdued, Yi ​cleared the earth ​of the ‌beasts the drought ​had unleashed: Yàyǔ, ‌Záochǐ, Jiǔyīng, Dàfēng, ​the serpent Xiūshé, ‌and the boar ​Fēngxī.

### The ‌Elixir

Xīwángmǔ's gift ‌of immortality, earned ​by the archer's ​service — and ​lost when Cháng'é ​drank it and ‌rose to the ‌cold palace of ​the moon.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography associated ‌with ‌Hòuyì ​concentrates in ​a ​small set ​of ​recurring ‌attributes, each ​a ​compressed ‌statement about ​the ‌name:[^1]

- ​**The ‌great ​bow and ​arrows** ​— Heaven-sent ​precision; ​the ‌power to ​correct ‌cosmic ​disorder without ‌destroying ​the cosmos
‌- ​**The ‌three-legged crow** ​— ​The true ‌form ‌of ‌each sun; ​nine ​were ‌shot down, ​and ​the tenth ‌still ​crosses ​the sky
‌- ​**The Fusang ‌tree** ​— ​The cosmic ​mulberry ​at the ‌eastern ‌edge ​of the ‌world ​where ​the ten ‌suns ‌roosted between ‌journeys
‌- ​**The elixir ‌of ​immortality** — ​Xīwángmǔ's ​reward ‌and the ​pivot ​of ​loss — ‌the ​gift that ​carried ​Cháng'é ‌to the ​moon
‌- **The ​spared ‌sun** ​— Measured ‌judgment; ‌the ​hero preserves ​the ​order he ​restores ‌rather ‌than abolishing ​it

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The cycle of ​Hòuyì is the great Chinese ‌myth of cosmic correction: a ‌heaven that gives too much, an ​earth that suffers for it, ​and one archer whose arrows ​restore the mean. Its episodes ​run from the scorched world ​of the ten suns to the ‌cold moon where his wife ​still dwells.[^1]

### The Shooting ​of the Nine Suns (Shanhaijing ‌/ Huainanzi)

In the reign ​of Emperor Yáo, the ten suns ‌— three-legged crows roosting in ​the Fusang tree, sons of ‌Dìjùn and the sun-mother Xīhé ​— abandoned their orderly rotation ​and rose together. The earth burned: ​rivers dried, crops withered, and ​the people starved. Yáo called ​on *Hòuyì*, the divine archer, ‌who climbed to the heights ​and loosed his arrows. One by ‌one nine suns fell from ​the sky in their crow ‌forms, and the tenth — ​spared — resumed its solitary, ‌lawful journey. The myth is told ​across the *Shān Hǎi Jīng* ‌tradition and given its fullest ​early form in the *Huáinánzǐ*.[^2]

​### The Clearing of the ‌Monsters (Huainanzi)

The drought had ‌loosed terrors on the world, and ‌the *Huáinánzǐ* lists the archer's ​second labor: he slew *Yàyǔ*, ​the man-eating beast of the ‌wilds; *Záochǐ* in the waters ​of Chouhua; *Jiǔyīng*, the nine-headed monster ​of the Xiong river; the ‌great wind-bird *Dàfēng* in the ​marshes of Qingqiu; the giant ​serpent *Xiūshé* at Lake Dongting; ‌and the monstrous boar *Fēngxī* in ​the mulberry groves of Sanglin. ‌Only when the last beast ​fell could the people plow ​in peace.

### The Elixir ​and the Flight of Cháng'é (Huainanzi)

​For his service, *Xīwángmǔ*, Queen ‌Mother of the West, granted ‌Hòuyì the elixir of immortality. ​He brought it home — ‌and there the story turns. His ​wife *Cháng'é* took the elixir ​and rose to the moon, ‌leaving the archer mortal and ‌alone on the earth he ‌had saved. Early versions are ‌spare about her motive; later tellers ​made her a thief, a ‌fugitive, or a wife protecting ​the elixir from the archer's ​treacherous disciple. However it is ​told, this is the hinge of ‌the cycle: the hero of ​the suns becomes the earthbound ​husband of the moon.

### ​The Betrayal of Féngméng (Mengzi ‌and Later Tradition)

The darker strand ​of the cycle is preserved ​already in the *Mèngzǐ*, which ​records that *Féngméng* (逢蒙) studied ‌archery under Yì and, once ​he had learned all that Yì ‌could teach, killed his master ​— in the fuller later ‌accounts, clubbing him to death ​with a peachwood staff. The ‌student murders the teacher the moment ‌the teaching is complete. The ​*Mèngzǐ* itself weighs how far ​Yì shared the blame for ​trusting such a man, and ​Chinese moralists have debated the lesson ‌ever since: mastery without loyalty ‌is the surest way to ​unmake a hero.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Hòuyì's myth ​traveled with ‌Chinese civilization ‌itself. In Japan ​the story ​of the archer ​and the ​ten suns ​was known through ‌Chinese texts ​and pictorial art, ​where it ‌informed depictions ​of solar catastrophe ‌alongside native ​Amaterasu lore; ‌Korea received the ​cycle through ​the same classical ​canon, and ​its own ​founding archer figure ‌Jumong — ​whose very name ‌is glossed ​as 'skilled ‌archer' — shows ​how deeply ‌the archer-hero type ​resonated on ‌the peninsula. ​Vietnamese tradition likewise ​absorbed the ‌ten-suns narrative ‌through Chinese literature. ‌Within China, ​Taoist tradition folded ​Yì into ‌its cosmology ​of solar regulation ​and immortality ‌elixirs, while the ​Queen Mother ​of the ‌West, his benefactor, ​rose to ‌become one ​of the highest ​deities of ​the Taoist pantheon. ​The myth ‌also furnished ‌Buddhist and popular ​writers with ‌a ready vocabulary ​for speaking ​of cosmic ‌excess and karmic ‌reversal, though ‌Yì himself ‌remained a figure ​of the ‌native classical tradition ​rather than ​a Buddhist ​convert. Scholars have ‌long noted ​the parallel with ​other great ​archers — ‌Apollo's plague-bringing arrows ​in Greece, ​Rama's bow in ​India — ‌but the ​Chinese version is ‌distinctive: the ​archer's target ‌is not a ​rival god ‌but disorder itself.[^1]

‌Within the ​Chinese tradition, ​closely related names ​in the ​corpus include [[bagua|Bāguà]], ‌[[change|Cháng'é]], [[fuxi|Fúxī]], ‌[[guandi|Guāndì]], [[guanyin|Guānyīn]], ​and [[long|Lóng]].

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: Hòuyì ​never left ‌the ‌Chinese imagination. ​The shooting ​of ​the suns ​is ​among the ‌first myths ​Chinese ​children learn, ‌retold ​in primers, ‌animated ​films, and ‌television dramas, ​and ​the Cháng'é ​sequel ​anchors the ​Mid-Autumn ‌Festival, when ​families gaze ‌at ​the moon ‌where ​the archer's ‌wife is ​said ‌to dwell. ​Modern ​China has ‌written ‌the pair ‌onto the ​sky ​itself: the ‌national ​lunar exploration ​program ‌is named ​*Cháng'é*, and ​its ‌missions are ​spoken ‌of as ​the moon ​goddess ​finally receiving ​visitors ‌— a ‌deliberate ​bridal of ‌myth and ​engineering. ​The idiom ‌of ‌'shooting the ‌suns' ‌survives as ​a metaphor ‌for ​cutting down ​excess ​and correcting ‌what has ​grown ​monstrous. In ​art, ‌from Han ​dynasty ​tomb reliefs ​to contemporary ‌illustration, ​the archer ‌drawing ​his bow ‌against ​a wheel ‌of suns ‌remains ​one of ​the ​most recognizable ​images in ‌the ‌Chinese visual ​canon.[^1]

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: Hòuyì's ​deeds are ‌textual before ‌they are ​pictorial. ​The earliest ​witnesses are ​Warring States ​literature: ‌the *Shān ​Hǎi Jīng* ​preserves the ‌ten-suns framework ​and ‌the suns' ​parentage, the ‌*Chǔ Cí* ​poem ​*Tiān Wèn* ​(Heavenly Questions, ​c. 4th–3rd ​century ‌BCE) interrogates ​Yì's shooting ‌of the ​suns ‌and his ​tangled fate, ‌and the ​*Mèngzǐ* ‌records the ​Féngméng betrayal. ​The fullest ‌surviving narrative ‌is ‌the *Huáinánzǐ* ​(139 BCE), ​which sets ‌the ​archer in ​Emperor Yáo's ‌reign and ​catalogs ​the slain ‌monsters. In ​Han dynasty ‌art ​the cycle ​became a ​staple of ​funerary ‌iconography: tomb ‌reliefs and ​painted stones ‌at ​sites such ​as the ‌Wu Liang ‌shrines (Shandong, ‌2nd ‌century CE) ​show the ‌archer drawing ​against ​crow-bearing suns, ​while Mawangdui ‌funerary art ​(168 ​BCE) depicts ​the solar ‌crow and ​the ​moon's toad-and-hare ​company that ‌would gather ​around ‌Cháng'é. Han ​mirrors and ‌later pictorial ​stones continued ‌the ‌imagery, fixing ​the bow, ​the crows, ​and ​the moon ‌as the ‌archer's permanent ​attributes.[^1]

sections.label: Classical Texts
sections.body: The ​archer's ‌dossier is ‌among ​the ​oldest in ​the ​corpus. ​The ‌*Tiānwèn* (Heavenly ​Questions) ​of ‌the *Chǔ ​Cí* ‌— ​a ‌catechism of ​riddles ​posed ​to the ​myths ​themselves ‌— ​asks why ‌Yì ​shot ‌the suns ​and ‌whom ​the ‌great crow's ​fall ​served.[^1] ‌The *Huáinánzǐ* ‌(c. ‌139 ​BCE) ​gives the ‌fullest ​early ​narrative: in ‌Yáo's ​reign ​the ‌ten suns ​rose ‌together, ​and ​Yì shot ​down ​nine, ‌then cleared ‌the ​earth ‌of ​its drought-born ​monsters.[^2] ‌The ‌*Mèngzǐ* preserves ‌the ‌dark ​ending ‌— the ​pupil ​Féngméng, ​having learned ‌all ​Yì ​could ​teach, murdered ‌his ​master ​— while ​the ‌*Zuǒzhuàn* ​records ‌a second, ​historical ‌Hòu ​Yì, the ‌Xia-dynasty ‌usurper, ​whom ​the tradition ​long ​entangled ‌with the ‌mythic ​archer.[^3]

sections.label: Daoist Sources
sections.body: Daoist ​tradition ‌keeps the ‌archer ​where ​the ​*Huáinánzǐ* put ​him: ​at ‌the ​threshold of ​the ‌immortality ​complex. ‌The ​elixir he ‌wins ​from ​[[xiwangmu|Xīwángmǔ]] ​is the ​canon's ​own ‌substance ​— the ‌Queen ​Mother's ‌drug ​of deathlessness ‌— ​and ‌his ​failure to ​keep ‌it ‌became ‌the ​standing parable ​of ‌the ​elixir ​that demands ‌more ​than ​merit: ‌the work ​must ‌be ​guarded, ​sealed, and ​inwardly ​digested, ‌or ‌it flies ​to ‌the ​moon.[^1] ​Later ‌hagiography enrolled ‌him ‌among ‌the ​transcendents, and ‌the ​ten-suns ​cosmology ​he corrected ‌— ​the ​solar ​crows roosting ‌in ​the ​Fúsāng ​tree — ‌supplied ​Daoist ‌liturgy ​and ‌art with ​their ‌standard ‌iconography ​of cosmic ​order ​restored ​by ‌a single ‌aligned ​agent.[^2]

sources.citation: Huáinánzǐ, elixir narrative; Daoist immortality complex.

sections.label: Buddhist Sources
sections.body: Buddhist ​cosmology ‌gave the ‌ten ​suns ​an ​apocalyptic ​echo. The ​Chinese ‌Buddhist ​canon ​describes the ‌kalpa ​of ‌destruction ​in which ‌suns ​multiply ​in ​the ​sky — ​two, ‌three, ​up ‌to seven ​— ‌until ​the ‌world ​burns: the ‌scene ​appears ​in ‌the cosmological ‌sūtras ‌translated ​into ​Chinese, and ‌medieval ​readers ​could ‌not ​help hearing ​Yì's ‌crisis ​in ‌it.[^1] The ​archer's ​answer ​is, ​of ‌course, un-Buddhist ‌— ​one ‌act ​of violence ​restoring ‌the ‌mean ‌— and ‌the ​contrast ‌is ​itself ​instructive: where ​the ‌sūtras ​wait ​out the ​fire, ‌the ​myth ​sends ​an archer. ‌The ​sun-crow ‌(三足烏) ​of his ‌story ​passed ‌into ‌the shared ​Buddhist-Daoist ​iconographic ​pool ​of ‌East Asian ‌art ​regardless.[^2]

sections.label: Calligraphy & Script
sections.body: 后羿 ​is ‌a ‌title before ​it ​is ​a ​name: ​后 ‌is the ​archaic ​graph ‌for ​'sovereign, ‌lord' ​— the ‌same ​word ​the ​*Shijing* ​uses ​of the ‌royal ​ancestors ‌— ​and ‌羿 is ​the ‌archer's ​own ‌name-graph, ​written ​with 羽 ‌(feather, ‌the ‌fletching) ​above ​廾. ‌'Lord Yì', ​the ​Sovereign ‌Archer.[^1] ​The ​distinction ‌matters in ​the ‌sources: ​the ​Xia-dynasty ​usurper ​of the ‌*Zuǒzhuàn* ‌is ​后羿 ‌by ​office, ​while the ‌sun-shooting ‌culture ‌hero ‌is ​also ‌called 夷羿, ​Yì ​of ​the ‌eastern ​Yí. Modern ​typography ​tempts ‌the ​eye ​toward ​後 ('after'), ‌a ​different ‌character ​altogether ‌— ​one of ‌the ‌small ​traps ​the ​restoration ​of 后 ‌must ‌explicitly ​avoid.[^2]

sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Hòuyì ​teaches the ‌hardest lesson ‌of ​heroism: that ​power must ​know ​when to ​stop. Nine ‌arrows ​were justice; ​a tenth ‌would have ​been ‌annihilation. The ​archer's greatness ‌lies ​not in ​what he ​destroyed ​but in ​the one ‌sun ​he spared ‌— the ​judgment ‌that the ​world needs ‌light, ​only not ‌too much ​of ​it. Chinese ‌thought found ‌in this ‌a ​parable of ​the mean: ‌excess, ​even of ​a good ‌thing, ​is the ​true monster, ‌and ​correction, not ‌eradication, is ​the ​hero's work.

​And yet ​the ‌myth refuses ‌him a ​clean ‌triumph. The ​savior of ​the earth ‌loses ‌immortality, loses ‌his wife, ‌and ​in the ‌darker telling ​dies ​at the ​hand of ‌his ​own student. ​To name ​a ‌domain *Hòuyì* ​is to ​claim ​that double ‌inheritance: the ​steadiness ‌to draw ​the bow ‌against a ​burning ‌sky, and ‌the humility ​to ​accept that ​even perfect ​aim ‌cannot hold ‌everything it ​wins.[^1]
